sections.html:
Lynchburg is an independent city in central Virginia, in the Blue Ridge foothills on the James River. It sits at about 630 feet of elevation and covers 49.53 square miles, nearly all of it land.

The city is bordered by Amherst County to the northeast, Bedford County to the west and northwest, and Campbell County to the south and southeast. The 2020 census counted 79,009 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 81,347, which makes Lynchburg the 11th-largest city in Virginia.

Because it is an independent city, Lynchburg has no county government above it. Assessments, tax bills and building rules all come from city offices.

sections.h2: Why is Lynchburg called the City of Seven Hills?
sections.html:
Lynchburg earned the nickname because the city spreads over seven hills: College Hill, Garland Hill, Daniel's Hill, Federal Hill, Diamond Hill, White Rock Hill and Franklin Hill. That terrain matters to a house, since steep lots mean retaining walls, long driveways and drainage runs that a flat city does not have.

John Lynch, a Quaker ferry operator, started a ferry across the James River, and the settlement grew around it after 1757. Virginia's General Assembly recognized the town in 1786, and it was incorporated as a city in 1852. Tobacco and river trade built the early economy, and Wikipedia notes that Lynchburg was the only major Virginia city not recaptured by Union forces before the Civil War ended.

sections.h2: What are the historic districts and neighborhoods in Lynchburg?
sections.html:
Lynchburg has a long list of local and state historic districts, and many houses in them are old. Wikipedia names these districts:

  • Court House Hill and Downtown
  • Daniel's Hill, Diamond Hill, Federal Hill and Garland Hill
  • Fifth Street, Kemper Street, Lower Basin, Pierce Street and Twelfth Street
  • Rivermont

Older houses in these areas often have original wood windows, plaster walls and old wiring or plumbing. Repairs there can cost more than in a house built last decade. If you own one and need to sell, the age of the house is the first thing most buyers will ask about. Ask the city planning office about any design review that applies before you start exterior work.

Lynchburg is a regional hub for education and manufacturing. Wikipedia lists nuclear technology, pharmaceuticals and material handling among the industries in the metro area, and it credits many small businesses with keeping the economy stable through downturns.

Higher education is a major part of the local picture. The city is home to Liberty University, the University of Lynchburg, Randolph College, Virginia University of Lynchburg and Central Virginia Community College. Lynchburg City Public Schools serves the city, with E. C. Glass High School and Heritage High School as the two public high schools.

With several campuses in town, some Lynchburg houses are rentals. A landlord who is tired of turnover and repairs between leases can choose to sell the house as it stands.

sections.h2: What does Lynchburg's weather mean for a house?
sections.html:
Lynchburg has four seasons with cool winters and hot, humid summers. The average January temperature is 35.9 degrees and July averages 76.0 degrees, according to the 1991 to 2020 normals.

Snow averages 11.6 inches a season, and some winters are much heavier. The snowiest on record, 1995 to 1996, brought 56.8 inches. A heavy winter like that is a reminder to have the roof and heating system looked at before you sell.

The city sits along the James River. If your house is near the river or a creek, check the flood map and ask your insurance agent before you list.

sections.h2: How does Lynchburg assess real estate?
sections.html:
The City Assessor values every parcel and sets a new value every two years. The office keeps a tax roll for July 1 through June 30 under Chapter 18-48 of the Lynchburg City Code and Title 58.1 of the Virginia Code.

The assessor's office page lists a 2025 to 2026 tax rate of $0.84 per $100 of assessed value. On a house assessed at $200,000, that rate works out to $1,680 a year. The figure is shown only as a worked example and is not a bill for any real property.

The office is at 900 Church Street, Lynchburg, VA 24504, open Monday through Friday from 8:30 am to 5 pm. The phone number is 434-455-3830. The city also runs an online ParcelViewer with property details and maps.

This page does not list due dates or appeal deadlines for Lynchburg. Ask the Assessor or the Treasurer's office for the current dates, since they can change.

sections.h2: How do roads and rail connect Lynchburg?
sections.html:
Lynchburg is near the geographic center of Virginia, and its transport links are strong for a city of its size. Greater Lynchburg Transit Company runs the local bus service and the campus shuttle at Liberty University.

Kemper Street Station, at 825 Kemper Street, serves Amtrak and Greyhound. The Crescent and a Northeast Regional train stop there, and the Northeast Regional connects Lynchburg with Washington and points north. Two Norfolk Southern lines cross in the city, and CSX also has a presence.

For a seller, a house close to the station or the main bus routes can appeal to commuters and students who prefer not to drive.

sections.h2: What does it take to sell a Lynchburg house for cash?
sections.html:
A cash sale is a normal Virginia closing without the loan step. The seller signs a contract, a settlement company searches the title, and the deed is recorded with the circuit court clerk.

  • Gather the deed, the tax bill and any payoff statements.
  • Ask the Assessor's Office about the current value on file.
  • Choose a closing date that fits your move.

Virginia puts a grantor tax of 50 cents per $500 of value on the deed, paid by the seller unless the contract shifts it. The deed must state the price on its first page to be recorded. Your settlement agent can confirm the exact charges.

sections.h2: What do Lynchburg sellers usually run into?
sections.html:
Lynchburg sellers tend to face a short list of issues, many tied to the age of the housing stock and the hills.

  • Old houses in historic districts that need major repairs.
  • Rental houses with turnover and unpaid repairs.
  • Inherited houses with out-of-town heirs.
  • Steep lots with drainage and foundation problems.

Selling directly lets you skip repair negotiations and keep the timing in your hands.

faqs.a: No. Lynchburg is an independent city, and it borders Amherst, Bedford and Campbell counties. City offices handle assessments and taxes.

faqs.q: What is the Lynchburg real estate tax rate?
faqs.a: The City Assessor lists $0.84 per $100 of assessed value for 2025 to 2026. Rates are set each year, so check the current figure with the city.

faqs.q: How often does Lynchburg reassess property?
faqs.a: The City Assessor says all parcels are reassessed every two years. Transfers and building permits are processed throughout the year.

faqs.q: Where do I call about my Lynchburg assessment?
faqs.a: Call the City Assessor's Office at 434-455-3830. It is at 900 Church Street and open Monday through Friday, 8:30 am to 5 pm.

faqs.q: Do I pay tax when I sell a Lynchburg house?
faqs.a: Virginia charges a grantor tax of 50 cents per $500 on the deed, and the seller usually pays it. Ask your settlement agent about any income tax question, since this page does not cover it.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Lynchburg house in a historic district?
faqs.a: Yes. Any house can be sold as is, though design review rules may apply to exterior changes. Ask the city planning office about the rules for your block.
